strengths: ParticleGS addresses a useful problem: future-view synthesis from observed videos without manually specifying material properties, forces, or governing physical equations. Combining Gaussian rendering with a shared evolving latent state provides a coherent, end-to-end approach.

The synthetic extrapolation improvements are substantial and consistent. ParticleGS achieves the highest extrapolation PSNR on all six Dynamic Object sequences and all four Indoor Scene sequences. Examples include Shark at 38.167 dB versus 30.904 for the strongest baseline, and Factory at 33.568 versus 25.415.

The comparisons include relevant forecasting methods, NVFi and GaussianPrediction, alongside reconstruction baselines. Reporting reconstruction separately helps contextualize extrapolation quality, and Figure 3 supports improvements in both predicted motion and visual detail.

Table 4 supports contributions from the latent representation, Neural ODE, and affine decoder. Although the evidence does not establish every claimed mechanism, the demonstrated forecasting gains provide a stronger case for acceptance than rejection.
weaknesses: The attribution of the gains to learning differential equations is only partially established. Without the Neural ODE, extrapolation PSNR remains 33.790 versus 34.224 on Dynamic Objects and 28.658 versus 29.772 indoors, retaining much of the advantage over prior methods. The replacement used in this ablation is unspecified, and the severe reconstruction collapse without latent space confounds representation capacity with dynamics learning.

Claims of physically plausible motion and stable extrapolation exceed the technical evidence. Equation 6 evolves a shared global feature with explicit time dependence, while local features remain fixed; it does not explicitly model particle interactions. Independently predicted affine transformations in Equation 7 do not guarantee local consistency or physical validity. These are reasonable architectural biases, but image metrics alone do not establish recovery of underlying physical laws.

Real-world evidence is mixed. On PanopticSports, the average extrapolation PSNR advantage over GaussianPrediction is approximately 0.28 dB, while LPIPS is worse on every sequence. Evaluation forecasts only the final 10% of each sequence, and the appendix explicitly omits qualitative results for this dataset. Thus, the broad claim of significantly superior extrapolation is much better supported synthetically than on real motion.

Reproducibility is incomplete despite the appendix. Important details include unspecified RK4 integration steps, actual FPS/KNN group sizes, optimization learning rates, and the precise affine decomposition described in Appendix A.1. Ablation implementations and baseline adaptations are also insufficiently documented, and the abstract's code-availability statement has no URL.

The originality discussion overstates limitations of prior methods. In particular, the assertion that GNNs cannot represent system evolution is not justified, and GaussianPrediction already addresses motion extrapolation. The defensible novelty is the specific end-to-end latent-ODE Gaussian framework. Likewise, performance at one temporal split per dataset does not establish the claimed stability across longer forecasting horizons.

strengths: The paper addresses a useful problem: future-view rendering from observed multiview videos without manually specifying physical equations, materials, or forces. Combining a shared latent Neural ODE with local Gaussian features provides a coherent, end-to-end approach to scene-specific motion extrapolation.

The synthetic results are substantial. ParticleGS achieves the highest extrapolation PSNR on all ten scenes in Tables 1–2, including 38.167 versus 30.904 for the strongest baseline on Shark and 33.568 versus 25.415 on Factory. Comparisons include both reconstruction methods and dedicated extrapolation methods, and the qualitative examples support improvements in object placement and rendering.

The evaluation includes six real-world sequences, reconstruction and extrapolation metrics, and component ablations. Table 4 shows that the complete architecture consistently improves extrapolation PSNR over the reported variants. These constitute meaningful empirical merits despite the limitations below.
weaknesses: The central explanation—that learning differential equations is responsible for the large extrapolation gains—is insufficiently isolated. In Table 4, removing the Neural ODE reduces extrapolation PSNR only from 34.224 to 33.790 on objects and from 29.772 to 28.658 indoors, retaining much of the improvement over prior methods. The replacement architecture is not described, and removing latent space also severely damages reconstruction, confounding representation quality with dynamics modeling. The ablations support the complete system more clearly than the claimed mechanism.

Physical plausibility and stable extrapolation are asserted more strongly than demonstrated. Equation 6 specifies a time-dependent neural vector field without a stability constraint; Equation 7 permits independent affine parameters and translations for each Gaussian without an explicit consistency constraint. Neither construction establishes recovery of physical laws. Image metrics and selected frames do not validate the claimed geometric correctness or long-horizon stability, and no trajectory errors or performance-versus-horizon analysis are reported.

Real-world evidence is mixed. Against GaussianPrediction, the average extrapolation PSNR improvement is approximately 0.28 dB, while LPIPS is worse on all six PanopticSports sequences. For example, Juggle improves from 24.316 to 25.158 PSNR but worsens from 0.166 to 0.225 LPIPS. Evaluation uses only the final 10% of each sequence, and Appendix A.3 explicitly omits real-world qualitative comparisons. Thus, broad claims of significantly superior future rendering exceed the demonstrated real-world advantage.

Important reproducibility details remain missing despite Appendix A.1: RK4 step size, FPS center and neighborhood counts, optimizer and learning-rate settings, and the exact affine decomposition used by the decoder. The appendix additionally mentions appearance decoding absent from the main formulation. Baseline training configurations and the ablation replacements are insufficiently specified, and the abstract's promised code link is blank.

The originality discussion overstates distinctions from prior work. The assertion that GNNs cannot represent temporal system evolution is not technically justified, and using a Neural ODE does not itself establish discovery of dynamical laws. The defensible contribution is the particular integration and its empirical results. Overall, the strong synthetic evidence makes this a borderline submission rather than a clear rejection, but incomplete methodological specification and insufficient support for the central dynamics claims prevent a stronger recommendation.

strengths: ParticleGS offers a useful approach to scene-specific 3D motion extrapolation: evolving a shared global latent state with a Neural ODE, combining it with local Gaussian features, and decoding Gaussian deformations. The pipeline learns from rendered-image supervision without requiring prescribed material properties, forces, or physical equations.

The synthetic extrapolation results are strong and consistent. ParticleGS achieves the highest extrapolation PSNR on all six Dynamic Object scenes and all four Dynamic Indoor scenes. Examples include 38.167 versus 30.904 dB for the strongest baseline on Shark, and 33.568 versus 25.415 dB on Factory. These comparisons include dedicated extrapolation methods NVFi and GaussianPrediction.

Figure 3 and the supplementary visual comparisons support improvements in future object placement and appearance, complementing the image metrics. Reporting reconstruction separately also helps expose differences in the underlying scene representations.

The balance favors weak acceptance: the substantial synthetic gains establish practical value for visual forecasting, despite incomplete attribution of those gains and weaker evidence for general physical dynamics.
weaknesses: The central Neural ODE contribution is insufficiently isolated. In Table 4, removing it reduces extrapolation PSNR only from 34.224 to 33.790 dB on objects and from 29.772 to 28.658 dB indoors, retaining much of the advantage over prior methods. The replacement used in this ablation is unspecified, and removing the latent space also severely damages reconstruction. These experiments do not cleanly establish that learning differential equations is the main source of improvement.

Real-world extrapolation results are mixed. In Table 3, ParticleGS improves average PSNR over GaussianPrediction by approximately 0.28 dB, but has worse LPIPS on every sequence; Tennis PSNR is slightly worse and Basketball is tied. Evaluation covers only the final 10% of each sequence, and no real-world qualitative results are provided. This supports modest short-term gains rather than uniformly superior real-world forecasting.

Claims of learning physically plausible dynamics and ensuring stable extrapolation exceed the evidence. Equation 6 evolves one global latent vector while local features remain fixed, and independently decoded per-Gaussian affine transformations do not themselves enforce physical consistency. No trajectory, geometry, physical-consistency, or error-versus-horizon analysis establishes the stronger interpretation of the learned representation.

Important reproducibility details remain missing despite Appendix A.1: the RK4 step size, latent dimensions, FPS/KNN group sizes, optimizer settings, and precise affine-component parameterization are not fully specified. The abstract's code-availability statement has no URL. Runtime and memory measurements are also absent, leaving the practical cost of ODE integration unclear.

The novelty discussion overstates distinctions from earlier work. The assertion that GNNs cannot represent temporal system evolution is not justified, and describing prior dynamic reconstruction methods as reconstructing frames independently overlooks their temporal representations. The defensible novelty is the particular end-to-end integration of latent ODE dynamics with Gaussian rendering, rather than a general exclusive ability to learn dynamics.

Some presentation claims do not match the tables: Section 5.2 reports approximately 0.1 dB reconstruction improvement over Grid4D for both Fan and Telescope, whereas Fan improves by 1.800 dB. Reconstruction quality is also not uniformly comparable to the strongest baseline, notably on Fallingball. These are correctable reporting issues, separate from the methodological concerns above.

strengths: ParticleGS makes a useful contribution to dynamic 3D scene extrapolation by combining Gaussian rendering with a compact, evolving latent state. Sharing system-level dynamic fields while retaining particle-specific static features is a sensible way to avoid integrating a separate high-dimensional state for every Gaussian.

The empirical gains are substantial on synthetic benchmarks. Extrapolation PSNR reaches 36.471 on Dynamic Objects versus FreeGave's 33.632, 31.103 on Dynamic Indoor Scenes versus TRACE's 29.476, and 36.136 on Dynamic Multipart versus FreeGave's 33.526. Comparisons include relevant extrapolation methods, not just reconstruction baselines.

Table 4 provides meaningful component ablations. Replacing the ODE evolver with a parameter-matched MLP reduces extrapolation PSNR from 36.471 to 34.551 on objects and from 31.103 to 27.455 on indoor scenes. The field-count and unfactorized-state experiments also support the compact representation's practical value.

The evaluation spans 20 scenes across four datasets, includes real videos, and reports per-scene results in the supplement. Figures 4–5 visibly support improved alignment and detail. Reported speeds of approximately 37–44 FPS suggest practical usefulness, subject to clarification of the timing protocol.

Overall, the demonstrated extrapolation improvements and supporting ablations favor acceptance. The strongest supported contribution is an effective latent-dynamics architecture for Gaussian scene prediction; this remains valuable despite reservations about its physical interpretation.
weaknesses: The central claim of learning physical laws is stronger than the evidence supports. Equations 8–12 define an unconstrained latent ODE trained through image reconstruction, without identifying physical quantities or enforcing physical consistency. The higher-order-to-first-order conversion establishes representational possibility, but does not show that the learned fields represent successive derivatives. Because the evolver can also depend explicitly on time, it can still encode a scene-specific trajectory. Rendering metrics and smooth latent visualizations establish predictive quality, not recovery of governing laws.

The experimental controls do not fully isolate the claimed advantage of higher-order physical modeling. The parameter-matched MLP ablation is useful, but its inputs and update mechanism are insufficiently specified. A controlled recurrent or velocity-based evolver using the same encoder, decoder, and training schedule would better distinguish benefits of integration, latent capacity, and optimization. Velocity-field formulations are not inherently incapable of representing accelerating trajectories.

Evidence for stable extrapolation is confined to the final 25% of each sequence. There are no error-versus-horizon curves, longer rollouts, or geometric/trajectory measurements to substantiate the stronger stability and physical-consistency claims. Real-world gains are modest: PSNR improves from 26.510 to 26.789 over FreeGave, with regressions on Wrist Rest. Without repeated runs, the reliability of these smaller gains is unclear.

Reproducibility remains incomplete despite useful architecture and training-stage details in the supplement. The RK4 step size or integration schedule, learning rates, exact temporal warm-up schedule, and inputs to the ODE-replacement ablation are not specified. The FPS protocol also does not establish whether encoding and integration are included, whether states are cached, or how runtime scales with prediction horizon. RK4 requires multiple derivative evaluations per step, making the stated 'single forward evaluation' explanation ambiguous.

Equation 10 has a concrete inconsistency with the stated rigid-motion interpretation: x_t = x + Rod(R)x + T gives x_t = 2x when R and T are zero, since the supplement defines Rod(0) as the identity. The intended transform or residual convention needs clarification. This appears correctable and does not alone invalidate the results, but it obscures the implemented decoder. Separately, the claim of best reconstruction performance across all datasets is overstated: Table 2 gives DeformGS slightly higher real-world reconstruction PSNR.

strengths: ParticleGS makes a useful contribution to dynamic scene extrapolation by combining a compact, shared latent dynamical system with Gaussian-specific static features and a deformation decoder. Evolving a small number of global fields addresses the computational burden of integrating individual Gaussian states.

The empirical support is substantial: evaluation covers 20 scenes across four datasets and includes relevant extrapolation baselines, particularly TRACE and FreeGave. Average extrapolation PSNR reaches 36.471, 31.103, and 36.136 dB on the three synthetic datasets, exceeding the strongest competing dataset averages by approximately 2.84, 1.63, and 2.61 dB. Figures 4–5 show corresponding improvements in predicted positions and appearance.

Table 4 provides useful component ablations. Replacing the ODE evolver with a parameter-matched MLP reduces extrapolation PSNR by 1.92 dB on Dynamic Objects and 3.65 dB on Dynamic Indoor Scenes. Field-count experiments support using a compact latent representation, and the reported 37–44 FPS indicates practical rendering performance.

Overall, the demonstrated extrapolation improvements and practical architecture favor weak acceptance. The evidence supports a useful learned motion representation, although the manuscript's stronger interpretation as physical-law discovery is not established.
weaknesses: The central physical interpretation exceeds the evidence. Equations 6–7 establish that higher-order dynamics can be represented by an augmented first-order system; they do not establish that the unconstrained learned fields recover derivatives, mass, material properties, or physical laws. The time-dependent evolver and flexible decoder can still fit a scene-specific trajectory. Image reconstruction losses, latent visualizations, and the toy spiral experiment do not demonstrate physical identifiability, conservation, or generalization to changed initial conditions.

Equation 10 is inconsistent with its stated rotation interpretation: x_t = x + Rod(R)x + T yields x_t = 2x when R and T are zero, since the appendix defines Rod(0) as the identity. This is not the usual rigid transformation or identity-preserving residual rotation. It may be a correctable equation error, but the manuscript leaves the implemented transformation and the interpretation of the physical-decoding ablation uncertain.

The evaluation establishes short-horizon continuation under a single 75%/25% temporal split, rather than stable physical extrapolation generally. There are no horizon-dependent error curves or quantitative trajectory/physical-consistency measurements. Real-world gains are modest: 26.789 versus 26.510 dB for FreeGave, with weaker results on Wrist Rest and Hammer. Without repeated runs, the robustness of these smaller differences is unclear.

The ablations do not fully isolate the claimed advantage of higher-order continuous dynamics. The replacement MLP's inputs and temporal update procedure are unspecified, and there is no matched recurrent/discrete latent dynamics comparison. Related neural-ODE scene methods are cited, but the discussion does not sharply distinguish the proposed dynamical formulation from existing latent-ODE approaches beyond its Gaussian representation and factorization.

Reproducibility and efficiency reporting remain incomplete despite useful architectural details in the supplement. RK4 integration step size, time normalization, learning rates, and the precise camera evaluation split are not specified. The FPS measurements do not clarify whether encoder computation and full ODE integration are included or how cost changes with prediction horizon. The claim of a single forward evaluation also needs clarification because RK4 requires multiple derivative evaluations per step.

strengths: ParticleGS offers a useful contribution to dynamic 3D reconstruction: a compact, shared latent dynamical system drives Gaussian deformation and enables future-frame prediction. Factorizing particle-specific static features from evolving global fields makes Neural ODE integration practical at Gaussian-scene scale.

The synthetic extrapolation results are strong against relevant prediction baselines. Tables 1–2 report PSNR improvements over the strongest competing dataset averages of approximately 2.84 dB on Dynamic Objects, 1.63 dB on Dynamic Indoor Scenes, and 2.61 dB on Dynamic Multipart. Reconstruction quality remains competitive, and Figures 4–5 show corresponding improvements in motion alignment and detail.

Evaluation covers 20 scenes across four datasets, including real video, and compares against both reconstruction and motion-extrapolation methods. Supplementary per-scene results provide useful transparency. Real-world improvements are modest but positive overall: 26.789 versus 26.510 PSNR and 0.150 versus 0.160 LPIPS against FreeGave.

Table 4 provides meaningful component ablations. Replacing the ODE evolver with a parameter-matched MLP reduces extrapolation PSNR by 1.92 and 3.65 dB on the two evaluated datasets. The field-count study supports using a compact latent representation, while reported rendering speeds of approximately 37–44 FPS demonstrate practical usefulness. These results collectively favor acceptance despite the reservations below.
weaknesses: The central claim of learning physical laws is stronger than the evidence supports. Equations 6–9 establish representational capacity, but an unconstrained latent ODE trained through image reconstruction does not establish that its coordinates represent physical quantities or that its dynamics obey physical laws. Equation 8 also explicitly permits time dependence. Feature visualizations and rendering metrics demonstrate predictive utility, not physical identification, conservation, or stability.

The mechanistic interpretation and originality are less convincing than the empirical contribution. Neural ODEs, latent-state factorization, attention aggregation, and Gaussian deformation are established components. The MLP ablation supports the proposed combination, but its inputs and rollout formulation are insufficiently specified; there is no comparably controlled recurrent or discrete state-transition baseline. Consequently, the experiments do not isolate continuous-time integration or the claimed higher-order dynamics as the source of improvement.

All evaluations use the first 75% of frames to predict the final 25%. This supports extrapolation over the tested interval, but not the broader claims of stable future dynamics. There are no horizon-dependent error curves, longer rollouts, or direct 3D motion/physical-consistency measurements. Real-world gains are small and nonuniform: ParticleGS trails FreeGave on Wrist Rest and TRACE on Hammer in extrapolation PSNR, with no repeated-run variability reported.

Equation 10 contains a concrete inconsistency with its physical interpretation: x_t = x + Rod(R)x + T gives x_t = 2x when R and T are zero, because Rodrigues' formula returns the identity matrix. This is not the stated rigid rotation-plus-translation update. Learned translation could compensate, so this need not invalidate the empirical results, but the equation and its relationship to the implementation require clarification.

Reproducibility and efficiency reporting remain incomplete despite useful architectural details in the supplement. The RK4 integration step size, learning rates, precise camera/frame sampling protocol, and baseline tuning are not specified. FPS measurements also lack a clear accounting of encoding and ODE integration costs, caching, and prediction horizon; training time and quantitative peak-memory comparisons are absent.
